rationale: Birkenholtz (2010) examines Jaipur's Asian Development Bank-backed water-supply reforms, centering primarily on full-cost-recovery pricing, connection fees, and rising-block tariffs (fees_tariffs_subsidies) alongside co-central public-private partnership restructuring (regulatory_model_ownership), incomplete decentralization and overlapping mandates between Urban Local Bodies and the state PHED under the 74th Constitutional Amendment (institutional_structure_coordination), and legal service mandates tied to slum regularization status (eligibility_status_documentation). Using a 2007 stratified household survey across six neighborhoods (reporting quantitative water availability and monthly household water expenditures in Table 2) combined with 2007 and 2009 qualitative interviews with households, PHED engineers, and tanker operators (mixed_methods), the paper evaluates both service intermittency, water quality, queuing/fetching burdens, and adaptive self-provisioning (effective_access) and class-stratified monthly household water expenditures and cost burdens (economic_access), as well as household versus standpost connection type (primary_connection) and utility cost-recovery deficits (administrative_outcome).
